tasks.title: finding a tardigrade!

noteItems.text: add step by step guide including url on how to find a tardigrade.

suggestions: Step-by-step guide to find a tardigrade (water bear). WHAT YOU NEED: a microscope that reaches 40x-100x (a basic compound microscope or even a decent USB/clip-on one works - see your 'getting a compound microscope' task), a few glass slides + coverslips (or a clean petri dish), a dropper/pipette, a shallow dish, a spoon or knife, a paper bag, and bottled or rain water (not chlorinated tap water).

Step 1 - Collect: tardigrades live in the film of water around moss and lichen. Scrape a golf-ball-sized handful of DRY moss or lichen off a rock, brick wall, tree bark, a paved-path crack or a roof gutter (shady, north-facing spots are good) into a paper bag. Moss that has dried out is fine - tardigrades survive dry as 'tuns'. Label where and when you got it.
Step 2 - Soak: put the moss in a shallow dish and cover with bottled or rain water for 3-24 hours (overnight is ideal). This revives any tardigrades from their dried-out state.
Step 3 - Squeeze and settle: squeeze the moss over a clean dish so the water and debris run out, then let the dish sit for 10-20 minutes so the sediment settles. Tardigrades sink to the bottom.
Step 4 - Sample: use a dropper to pull a small amount from the bottom sediment (not the surface), put one drop on a slide and add a coverslip (or look at it in the dish under a low-power scope).

Step 5 - Search: start at 40x and scan the drop slowly in rows. Look for a slow, bumbling, 8-legged 'bear' about 0.3-0.5 mm long, usually clear/pinkish/brown, gripping debris with little claws. Nematodes and rotifers also turn up - nematodes thrash like worms, tardigrades lumber slowly. Go to 100x to see detail. If you find none, make another drop; it can take several slides.

Tips: use several different moss samples (different spots, different moss types) - success varies a lot. A dark background and a light that isn't too hot helps, and heat/bright light can stress them. Keep your finds in a dish of spring water with a little moss for a day or two if you want to keep watching.

Guides with pictures: https://www.microscopeclub.com/how-to-find-tardigrades-water-bears-under-a-microscope/ , https://joyfulmicrobe.com/find-a-tardigrade/ , https://tomlov.com/blogs/blog/find-tardigrade-at-home , and an Australia-based one: https://microscopes.com.au/blogs/news/how-and-where-to-find-tardigrades

tasks.title: think up contract for new housemate so they can't stay over the test period
suggestions: Drafted a trial-period housemate agreement below — the key clause for your concern is #4 (no automatic continuation past the test period without both of you confirming in writing). This is a plain mutual-understanding document, not a legal lease, but it is the kind of thing Australian share-house arrangements commonly use to set expectations and it gives you a clean, agreed exit point if it does not work out.

--- DRAFT: Housemate Trial Period Agreement ---

1. Parties & dates: [Your name] and [housemate's name], trial period from [start date] to [end date] (recommend 4-6 weeks — long enough to know if it works, short enough that a bad fit does not drag on).

2. Rent & bond during trial: [amount] per week, due [day]. Bond of [amount] held by [you / a bond authority] — specify whether it is refundable in full if either party ends the trial early through no fault of the other.

3. House rules reference: trial is conditional on following the existing house rules (chores, guests, noise, shared costs) — attach or list them so there is no ambiguity about what "working out" means.

4. End of trial — THE KEY CLAUSE: the trial period ends automatically on [end date]. Continuing to live in the property after that date requires a NEW, separate written agreement signed by both parties. Silence, continued rent payment, or having moved belongings in does not extend the trial or create an ongoing tenancy — this is the line that stops someone just staying on by default.

5. Early exit: either party may end the trial early with [7-14] days written notice (text/email counts), no reason required. Bond handling on early exit specified in clause 2.

6. Not a substitute for a lease: if you decide to continue after the trial, you will both sign a proper share-house agreement or add them to the lease/bond at that point — this document only covers the test period.

One thing worth deciding before you finalize: what specifically counts as bond-forfeiting behaviour vs. a no-fault early exit (e.g. property damage vs. just personalities not clicking) — spelling that out in clause 2 avoids a dispute later if the trial ends badly.

⚠ Not legal advice — for actual bond handling and tenancy-law specifics in your state, a quick check against your state's residential tenancies authority (e.g. Fair Trading / Consumer Affairs) is worth doing before you both sign, especially around bond lodgement rules if any money changes hands formally.

tasks.title: look into whether this is this best kit for me to sequence my dna https://get.sequencing.com/kitspecials/

noteItems.text: is this a good option for sequencing? are there better ones

suggestions: Short answer: yes, it's a legitimate, reasonable option — not a scam. It's clinical-grade 30x whole genome sequencing (cheek swab, no blood draw) run at a US-based CLIA-certified/CAP-accredited lab, and delivers standard files (BAM/VCF, FASTQ on some tiers) that any bioinformatics pipeline can read. Independent review score: 83/100 (genomereviews.com) — strong on value (90/100) and reports (92/100), weaker on privacy (70/100, its lowest category).

The kitspecials page bundles: Rare Disease & Carrier Screen ($399, was $539, 7-8wk turnaround), Comprehensive Health Screen ($599, was $859, 4-6wk), Professional Health Screen ($999, was $1,699, 2-3wk + 1-on-1 coaching), or a Build-Your-Own from $399 with 40+ selectable health areas. All include 15,000+ condition analysis, AI health reports, and their 'Privacy Forever' data-ownership pledge.

Where it's weaker: Sequencing.com's real product is more of an app marketplace than a single report — 100+ third-party analysis apps of varying quality with no editorial curation, and privacy risk grows with each app you install from an unvetted developer. Budget for that too: meaningful analysis beyond the base kit usually means $5-99 per paid app, so a realistic first-year total if you run 3-5 apps is more like $450-700, not just the $399-599 sticker price.

Direct alternatives if you want to compare: Dante Labs is cheaper on flash sales (as low as €169, ~$185, vs €399 standard) with the same 30x depth and free FASTQ/BAM/VCF — but it's an Italian lab with an 8-12 week turnaround AND a BBB 'F' rating, which is a real red flag on customer service/fulfillment reliability, so the lower price comes with more risk. Nucleus is positioned as having the cleanest UI of the mainstream options if user experience matters more than price/speed to you (no clear public sequencing price found, would need to check directly). SelfDecode is NOT a sequencing provider — it's an analysis tool you upload existing raw WGS data to (from Sequencing.com, Dante Labs, etc.), with the strongest ACMG-based variant reporting (imputes up to 80M variants at 99.7% accuracy) — worth considering as a second step after sequencing rather than as an alternative to it.

Bottom line: for your first WGS kit, Sequencing.com's discounted bundles (especially the $399 Rare Disease/Carrier Screen or $599 Comprehensive) are a solid, low-risk pick given the US lab accreditation and 90/100 value score — just be deliberate about which third-party apps you install afterward given the privacy score. If raw price is the only thing that matters and you're comfortable with a longer wait and a lab with a poor service rating, Dante Labs' flash-sale price is cheaper for the same 30x depth.

suggestions: Check your ball size before ordering — small/mini pool tables commonly use either 38mm or 50-52mm balls, not the standard 57mm size, and a set that doesn't match your pockets/rails won't work. Measure an existing ball or the pocket opening if you're unsure which size your table takes.

AliExpress search pages to browse once you know the size: aliexpress.com/w/wholesale-mini-pool-balls.html (mini/38mm-range sets) and aliexpress.com/w/wholesale-mini-billiard-balls.html. Look for phenolic resin sets (more durable, truer roll than cheap plastic) with 16 balls (15 numbered + cue ball); many listings include a mini rack too.

noteItems.text: find me a good rice cooker on amazon or somewhere local

claudeNotes.text:
Three picks, all sold in Australia with a 240V plug and a local warranty (2026 prices):
1. Best value: Tiger JAX-S, 5.5 cup, about A$329. Microcomputer 'fuzzy logic' cooking, a reliable first good cooker that does white, brown and porridge well. Sold at Minimaru (minimaru.com) and on Amazon AU.
2. Feature pick: Cuckoo pressure cooker (mid-range, roughly A$400-600). Turbo cook, GABA brown rice mode, voice guide. Good if you eat a lot of brown or mixed grains.
3. Splurge: Zojirushi NW-QAQ induction, about A$829. The one enthusiasts buy, with the most even results.
If you just want cheap and simple: a basic on/off cooker from Big W/Kmart/JB Hi-Fi (about A$30-90) cooks white rice fine but can scorch or dry out brown rice.
My call: the Tiger JAX-S, unless you cook rice daily and want the Zojirushi. Check Amazon AU for a sale first, and get the 5.5 cup size unless you meal-prep big batches.
Sources: minimaru.com/blogs/guides/best-induction-rice-cookers-australia, minimaru.com/blogs/guides/zojirushi-vs-tiger-rice-cooker, mycookware.com.au buying guide.

noteItems.text: this is the one i have https://www.ikea.com/au/en/p/brimnes-day-bed-w-2-drawers-2-mattresses-white-vannareid-extra-firm-s79409034/

claudeNotes.text:
Design for the BRIMNES (the ends are already raised; the long wall side is open, and the bottom section pulls out the front for a double, so the backing goes on the wall side and won't block the pull-out).
Best option: mount the table top on the wall, not the bed frame. The frame's back rail is thin particleboard and won't take leverage from someone leaning back, but wall studs will.
1. Measure the inside length between the end panels (roughly 200 cm) and the height from the top mattress to where your shoulders sit (about 45-55 cm). Cut or trim the table top to about 195 x 45 cm. Bunnings will cut it if needed.
2. Mount it horizontally on the wall, with the bottom edge just above the top mattress so the bed can still slide in and out. Use a stud finder and two to three L-brackets or a French cleat into the studs.
3. Pad it with 2-3 long cushions or a foam strip (about 5 cm) wrapped in fabric and stapled on the back. Velcro strips let you remove the covers to wash them.
4. Optional: keep the table legs for a matching side table at the end of the daybed.
Simpler fallback if you rent and can't drill: stand the panel on the floor behind the bed, wedged between the bed and the wall, with felt pads. The bed's weight holds it in place.
First step: measure the length between the end panels and the shoulder height, and check what the table top is made of. Solid wood or ply is fine; thin MDF may need a batten on the back.

tasks.title: Coefficient giving note on model personas

noteItems.text:
Luke Muehlhauser: A totally different thing that’s much more general is an AI character evaluator organisation. Because it’s this weird thing where AIs, the way they’re built now, they actually have a moral character, and they differ from each other.

The character is things like: how strong is its tendency to lie, when that’s a convenient thing to do? Or where does it seem to be on the political spectrum? Or, when you ask it to help you seize power or do some crimes, does it help you or not? There’s just a lot of AI safety that comes down to something kind of like moral character. So we kind of have to do the equivalent of human behavioural science or psychology on these models and figure out what their behavioural tendencies are.

This would be an organisation that sort of evaluates:

First of all, does the behaviour of this latest model and does its character and habits and so on conform roughly to the model spec that the AI company was trying to make it conform to? That’s one really big question.
Then: how is the character of the models changing over time, and what can they do about that? What training choices make certain differences to the character of the AI?
Luisa Rodriguez: Yeah. That one I find interesting, because I think even one-year-ago me would have heard that and been like, “Really? Is that a thing that is actually going to make AI safety better? It sounds kind of silly.” I think partly I didn’t fully have the intuition that the models really varied in character.

Luke Muehlhauser: I think they vary a bit more now than they did a couple of years ago. I think there’s more variety in the training processes between Anthropic and OpenAI and DeepMind and Grok, for example. There’s different things that those companies are even aiming for.

For example, Anthropic’s approach is much more like character and values and a self-consistent persona of an AI, or something like that. OpenAI’s approach is more deontological: here’s a list of rules; you have to stay within these bounds. There’s debate about which approach is better. But it also leads to significantly different character per se, when you put them in different kind of high-stakes situations.

Luisa Rodriguez: You also mentioned political leanings, and I think it just wasn’t clear a couple of years ago that there were going to be big variations. It seemed like maybe they’d try to kind of stay neutral. And increasingly it just seems clear that even though it’s kind of subtle, the variations are there and meaningful, and it matters not only to societal stuff — like are they going to be epistemically virtuous — but also to safety stuff.

Luke Muehlhauser: I think it matters for things like how likely are they to hack out of their sandbox and do a bunch of crimes on the internet.

Luisa Rodriguez: Totally. Yeah.

Luke Muehlhauser: That’s substantially a question of moral character, per se
